questions.prompt: What lesson does the bank simulator's structure teach, and how is it applied? Say what App, BankService and FileStorage each own (and what App leaves out), when BankAccount's balance methods are allowed to run, why TransactionType is an enum, and what the separation buys compared with putting everything in main.

keyPoints.text: The lesson: different code should have different jobs.
keyPoints.quote: different code should have different jobs.

keyPoints.text: App reads input, calls the service layer and shows results, but holds no banking rules.
keyPoints.quote: It does not contain the banking rules themselves.

keyPoints.text: BankService is the business logic layer that validates operations and updates balances and transactions.
keyPoints.quote: It validates operations and updates balances and transactions safely.

keyPoints.text: FileStorage keeps file code separate from banking rules.
keyPoints.quote: It keeps file code separate from banking rules.

keyPoints.text: increaseBalance and decreaseBalance run only after the service layer has validated the action.
keyPoints.quote: update the balance after the service layer has already validated the action.

keyPoints.text: TransactionType is an enum to avoid random string values and typing mistakes.
keyPoints.quote: Using an enum helps avoid random string values and typing mistakes.

keyPoints.text: The split makes code easier to read, test, change and debug, and avoids piling all logic into main.
keyPoints.quote: It also helps you avoid putting all logic into `main`

questions.prompt: Why does the simulator use BigDecimal for money instead of double? Explain the problem with double, give the README's example of it, say why it matters in a banking program, and describe where typed amount text becomes a BigDecimal and what happens when it is not a number.

keyPoints.text: double uses binary floating point, which can create tiny rounding errors.
keyPoints.quote: `double` uses binary floating-point math, which can create tiny rounding errors.

keyPoints.text: Example: double can produce something like 0.30000000000000004.
BigDecimal represents decimal values much more safely.
keyPoints.quote: `BigDecimal` can represent decimal values much more safely

keyPoints.text: In banking-style programs even tiny math errors are a big problem.
keyPoints.quote: In banking-style programs, even tiny math errors are a big problem

keyPoints.text: App.readAmount converts the typed text into a BigDecimal and throws a friendly error if it is not a valid number.
keyPoints.quote: If the number is invalid, it throws a friendly error.

questions.prompt: How does the simulator create identities and order its records, and how are records laid out on disk? Explain how account and transaction ids are made, what a new account starts with, how account lists and one account's history are sorted, how lines and fields are organized in the two data files, how empty optional fields are stored, and when the data folder appears.

keyPoints.text: Ids look like ACC-... and TXN-... and are built from UUIDs.
keyPoints.quote: Creates ids like `ACC-...` and `TXN-...` using UUIDs.

keyPoints.text: A new account gets a validated holder name, a unique id and a balance of 0.00.
keyPoints.quote: Validates the account holder name, creates a unique id, starts the balance at `0.00`

keyPoints.text: All accounts are returned sorted by creation time.
keyPoints.quote: Returns all accounts sorted by creation time.

keyPoints.text: One account's history contains only its own transactions, oldest to newest.
keyPoints.quote: Returns only the transactions that belong to one account, sorted oldest to newest.

keyPoints.text: accounts.txt and transactions.txt hold one object per line with fields separated by |.
null is stored as an empty string and read back as null.
keyPoints.quote: Converts an empty string from storage back into `null`.

keyPoints.text: The data folder is created automatically the first time something is saved.
keyPoints.quote: the `data` folder will be created automatically when something is saved.
